# Figure 1: A computational framework for comprehensively evaluating multispecific cell-type selectivity

::: {#fig-figure-1}

Overview of the multispecific cell-type-selectivity problem and the experimental and computational framework used to evaluate candidate receptor targets.
:::

## Outline

* Number of combinations to consider is huge: pairs/triads of receptors, all cell populations
* Methods of increasing complexity and computational cost:
  + Target/off-target distribution shape
  + KL divergence
  + W distance
  + The binding model.
* The experimental framework:
  + CITE-seq approximates surface protein expression at single-cell resolution
  + We define a set of possible surface targets pairs and target cell types
  + Some surface proteins are lowly expressed and have higher expression in off-target cells than target cells. These are filtered on a per-target-cell-type basis
  + For every target pair/target cell type combination, we evaluate selectivity based on EMD, KL divergence, and binding model

* In order to guide drug design, we needed a faithful predictor of the cell-type selectivity of a given combination of targets.
* In order to evaluate different predictors, we needed a faithful quantitative description of a large number of candidate target receptors.
* Given that a molecule's selectivity is largely determined by the distribution in expression of its cognate receptors across target and off-target cells, this description needed to be high resolution and defined across diverse cell types.
* Based on these criteria, we chose a CITE-seq dataset comprised of 230 unique surface proteins measured across 160,000 PBMCs spanning 30 distinct cell types.
* After filtering for lowly expressed proteins, we defined a set of 130 surface proteins that, together, comprise over 9,000 unique target pairs or 400,000 unique target triads. We then evaluated the selectivity of each target pair for all 30 cell types, resulting in over 270,000 unique target pair/cell type combinations.

* The vast combinatorial space of multispecific target combinations encouraged us to turn to computational techniques for efficient exploration. 
  + Effective tools for parsing this space must meet a series of key criteria. An effective tool must: 
    - be capable of evaluating the effect of targeting multiple receptors simultaneously, not just in isolation.
    - be computationally efficient enough to evaluate thousands of target combinations in a feasible time frame.
    - be invariant to the scale of a target's absolute expression because of the unreliability of state-of-the-art protein expression quantification methods.
    - be sensitive to heterogeneity in expression across target and off-target populations, which is a known determinant of cell-type selectivity [@tan2021-intbio].
* Given that heterogeneity in expression is a key indicator of a receptor's potential to be a selective target, we devised a series of computational approaches capable of efficiently quantifying the selectivity of a given set of targets from their mRNA or protein expression.
  + Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence is a computationally simple measurement of the information lost when one probability distribution is used to approximate another (@fig-KL-diagram).
  + Wasserstein distance (commonly referred to as Earth Mover's Distance; EMD) is a more complex optimal transport metric that measures the minimum cost of transforming one probability distribution into another (@fig-EMD-diagram).
  + KL divergence and EMD each quantify distinct statistical differences between a target protein's expression distribution in target and off-target cells, are both scale-invariant in at least one dimension, and can both be evaluate any number of target proteins targeted together through application to joint distributions of arbitrary dimensions.
  + To obtain a more flexible, mechanistic description of cell-type selectivity, we also optimized a previously published model of multivalent binding designed to predict equilibrium receptor binding of ligand complexes composed of varying numbers and kinds of binding subunits (@fig-multivalent-binding) [@tan2021-mathbiosci].
* To get the most out of these tools, we sought a comprehensive---yet faithful---representation of surface protein expression.
  + We chose a single-cell dataset of containing the protein expression of 228 surface proteins across 160,000 PBMCs, generated by Cellular Indexing of Transcriptomes and Epitopes by Sequencing (CITE-seq) [@Hao2018].
